analysis.one_liner: Requires every employer to provide basic health coverage to workers and their families.
analysis.headline: Waxman's employer-mandate health bill drew 20 Democratic cosponsors and two days of subcommittee hearings in October 1989, but no committee ever voted on it and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every employer to enroll each employee and their family in a health plan covering hospital care, doctor services, tests, prenatal and well-baby care, and mental health treatment, with no pre-existing-condition exclusions and strict caps on deductibles, copays, and out-of-pocket costs. New coverage would flow through state-certified "regional insurers" charging community-rated premiums that could not vary by age, gender, or health status. It would also require states to cover everyone below the poverty line starting in 1991, near-poverty residents by 1996, and everyone else by 1999, while subsidizing small businesses whose compliance costs ran above 5% of revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families who had no coverage, had pre-existing conditions, or faced unaffordable deductibles would get guaranteed, regulated coverage; workers earning under 125% of the minimum wage would be offered at least one plan with no employee premium; everyone below poverty would get benefits with no premiums, deductibles, or copays; doctors and hospitals would gain paying patients in place of unpaid bills; and small employers above the cost threshold would have 75% of their excess compliance cost reimbursed.

how_it_helps.text: Every employer would have to enroll each employee and their family in a health benefit plan, enforced by civil penalties of up to 10% of the employer's total wages and damages to employees for knowing violations.
Plans could not exclude or limit coverage for any pre-existing condition, and coverage would begin within 30 days of an employee's first hour of work.

Deductibles would be capped at $250 individual and $500 family (rising only with inflation), copays at 20% of cost, and out-of-pocket expenses at $3,000 per year (or 10% of wages), and any employee earning less than 125% of the minimum wage must be offered at least one plan with no premium.

Insurers in the new regional system would have to use community rating, barred from setting premiums based on age, gender, or expected use of services — the core anti-discrimination mechanism of the bill.

States would have to offer the same basic benefit package to everyone under the poverty line starting in 1991 with no cost-sharing, to near-poverty residents (up to 185% of poverty) by 1996, and to all other uncovered residents by 1999, with 30-day eligibility determinations and six months of guaranteed eligibility.
Small employers whose compliance cost exceeded 5% of gross revenues would be paid 75% of the excess, cushioning the mandate for the smallest firms.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — who would pay at least 80% of premiums for most plans and face penalties up to 10% of total wages for noncompliance; federal and state taxpayers, who would fund the Medicaid expansion and the small-business subsidies (the bill text specifies no dedicated funding source); and state and local governments, which would have to cover their own employees and would lose federal Public Health Service grants if they failed to comply. Workers would bear part of the cost indirectly if employers held down wages to absorb the new expense.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and federal and state taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost to employers: since employee premiums are capped at 20% of the actuarial rate, employers would pay at least 80% for most plans, and noncompliance carries a civil penalty of up to 10% of total wages — a burden that could slow hiring or wage growth, especially for firms that do not currently offer coverage.

The bill creates large new obligations — mandatory benefits for everyone below poverty, Medicare-level reimbursement rates for those services, and a 75% subsidy for small employers — but the text specifies no dedicated funding source for them, leaving the cost to federal and state budgets.
The phase-in is slow: near-poverty adults are not mandatorily covered until 1996 and everyone else until 1999, so full coverage would be a decade out from the 1989 introduction.

The bill channels universal coverage through private insurers rather than a public plan, and even compliant plans keep premiums, deductibles, copays, and coinsurance — including copays of up to 50% for outpatient mental health care — and cover no routine preventive care beyond prenatal and well-baby visits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people, the bill's gains were large and direct: guaranteed coverage with no pre-existing-condition exclusions, hard caps on cost-sharing, community-rated premiums, and free coverage for the poor. The honest costs fall on employers (a genuine new labor expense, potentially passed back as slower wage growth) and on taxpayers, and the bill was expensive by design — a phased, multi-year program with subsidies for small business and Medicare-level provider payments, all routed through private insurers with their administrative overhead. It was a serious, detailed attempt at universal coverage rather than a badly designed bill, but its cost and its reliance on an employer mandate were exactly the points around which the politics would have been hardest.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and their subcommittees — hearings in October 1989, then nothing — and expired when the Congress ended without any committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on April 12, 1989, joined by four original cosponsors and three more sponsors added in May.
The bill was referred jointly to the House Education and Labor and Energy and Commerce Committees on the day it was introduced, then split across four subcommittees within three weeks.
The subcommittees held hearings on October 11 and 12, 1989, and requested executive comment from the Labor and Health and Human Services Departments — the furthest the bill ever went.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died on January 3, 1991, when the 101st Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have borne the coverage mandate — especially the smallest and the firms that offered nothing — plus taxpayers who would have funded the new public benefits, are better off because the bill died; uninsured workers and families and people with pre-existing conditions gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid for coverage

for.name: Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through referral and subcommittee hearings as a senior member of the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: 20 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

for.name: Subcommittees of Education and Labor and of Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Held two days of hearings in October 1989 and requested comments from the Labor and HHS Departments, the only formal consideration the bill received.

against.name: House Education and Labor and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill; after the October 1989 hearings, no markup or committee vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed employer health insurance mandates, proposing tax-based approaches to coverage instead, setting the administration against the mandate model this bill embodied.

against.name: Employer and small-business lobbies (U.S. Chamber of Commerce, NFIB)
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against employer health insurance mandates during the 1989-1994 health reform debates.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 20 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican signing on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call ever split the chambers.

industries.note: The bill would guarantee insurers millions of new mandated customers by requiring every employer without a plan — and small employers that switch insurers — to buy from state-certified regional insurers, locking private carriers in as the permanent channel for universal coverage. In exchange it binds them to community rating, guaranteed issue with no pre-existing exclusions, cost-sharing caps, and possible competitive bidding if profits run 20% or higher, so their gain comes bundled with the public's gain.

Every employer would have to pay at least 80% of premiums for covered plans and face penalties up to 10% of total wages for noncompliance — a new cost for firms that currently offer nothing. Small employers get a partial cushion: 75% reimbursement of compliance costs above 5% of gross revenues.
Universal coverage would convert unpaid care into paid claims, and the new public program pays providers at no less than Medicare rates — providers gain as the uninsured gain.

Governments would have to enroll their own employees in plans and fund their share of the new Medicaid-based coverage, and any state entity that failed to comply would lose eligibility for Public Health Service Act grants, contracts, and loans.
